Bumble Romance Scams UK: Spot a Fake Profile or Con

Scammers on Bumble use fake profiles and emotional manipulation to trick people into sending money. Here's exactly how to protect yourself.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-05-08 · Updated 2026-08-09 · 9 min read

Quick answer: On Bumble, who sends the first message depends on the match and any Opening Move, so starting the chat proves nothing about the person replying. Keep the conversation in Bumble, use its Photo Verification request and in-app voice or video calls, never send money or follow investment advice, and report suspicious behaviour before unmatching.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

Who sends the first message, and why it proves nothing

On Bumble, who opens a conversation depends on the match. In heterosexual connections, women decide how the first move is made; where an Opening Move has been set, a match can reply to it regardless of whose move it otherwise is. In same-gender and non-binary matches, either person can start. Against everyday nuisance behaviour that works well.

Fraud is built around the rule rather than stopped by it. A scam account never needs to start a conversation; it only needs to be swiped right on. So the profile is engineered to be picked — warm photographs, a plausible profession, prompts that echo whatever the target says she is looking for — and then it waits.

There may be a cognitive trap in that, and it is worth naming as a possibility rather than an established Bumble-specific finding: it can be harder to re-examine somebody you feel you chose yourself. Whether or not that applies to you, the mechanical point stands on its own. Opening the conversation tells you nothing whatsoever about who is at the other end of it.

The 24-hour clock, and the urgency it hands a fraudster

A Bumble match expires if no one sends a message within 24 hours of matching. In ordinary use that keeps queues moving. Inside a scam it supplies urgency the fraudster never has to invent.

Watch how the deadline gets used.

  • 'Send me your WhatsApp before this expires' in the earliest exchanges. The countdown becomes the pretext for leaving the one place where moderation and reporting function.
  • Any framing that turns Bumble's timer into a reason you must answer tonight rather than tomorrow, or send something now rather than think about it.

The clock belongs to Bumble, not to them, and letting a match lapse costs very little. Every member gets one free Extend a day, which buys another 24 hours. Paid tiers can extend without limit, and Boost and Premium include Rematch, so a genuine connection is recoverable. A deadline is never a reason to make a decision you would otherwise take slowly.

Two different verifications, and what each one can prove

Bumble runs two checks that are easy to confuse, and the difference changes what you can conclude.

  • Photo Verification is a selfie check confirming that a member matches their profile photos. This is what Bumble Support's request feature triggers: you ask a match to verify, they receive a prompt to take a selfie, and an approved check shows on their profile.
  • ID Verification is optional in the UK, launched there in March 2025, and asks for a government-issued document plus a live selfie. Bumble's privacy policy names Veriff as its ID-check provider.

The request you can send inside the app is the Photo Verification one, so do not expect it to put a match through the full ID process. It is still the most useful single message you can send to anybody who will not get on a call. You can also filter your experience towards members who have verified.

Be clear about the ceiling on both. Verification can add confidence that the person in the photographs is the person typing. Neither check proves intentions, and neither tests a single financial claim anybody makes. Because verification is voluntary, a missing badge proves very little — plenty of genuine members never bother with it. A match who declines a verification request while declaring strong feelings has answered a different question, and answered it clearly.

Behind the scenes Bumble also runs Deception Detector, the machine-learning screen it introduced in 2024. Bumble says that in testing it automatically blocked 95 per cent of the accounts it had identified as spam or scam profiles — the denominator there is accounts Bumble's systems had already flagged, not every fraudulent account on the app. No automated tool guarantees that a profile is safe.

What UK police record as romance fraud

UK police describe dating and romance fraud as deceiving someone into a fictitious romantic relationship, often online, in order to gain their trust and exploit them financially. INTERPOL has asked organisations to stop using the 'pig butchering' nickname, which describes victims as livestock, and to use romance baiting instead — that is the term used here.

City of London Police figures published in May 2026 put UK romance-fraud losses at more than £102 million in 2025, across 10,784 reports, a 29 per cent rise on the year before. People aged 55 to 74 accounted for almost half of everything stolen. Men filed more reports overall, while women accounted for a larger share of the value lost.

Two things follow. Police guidance is explicit that romance-fraud victims are not to blame and should not feel ashamed or embarrassed, so making a report is a statement of fact rather than a confession. And the heaviest losses sit later in life, which is worth knowing if you are reading this about a parent rather than about yourself.

Testing a Bumble match without accusing anyone

Every check below fits inside an ordinary conversation.

  • Ask for a voice or video call inside Bumble rather than on another platform — Bumble provides both in the app. A refusal that survives two or three attempts is itself the finding.
  • Send a Photo Verification request and watch whether the answer is agreement or a story.
  • Keep talking in Bumble. If the account ever needs reporting, the messages are still sitting there for moderators to read.
  • Use Share Date before you meet: it tells a trusted contact who you are seeing, where and when, and can update them in the app if the plan changes.
  • Reverse-search the photographs. Uniformly polished images, no candid shots and nobody else in frame is a pattern worth noticing.
  • Notice who raises money first. Police guidance puts the test simply: any request for money from someone you know only online should ring an alarm bell — and that covers vouchers, cryptocurrency and investment opportunities exactly as much as it covers cash.

Reporting on Bumble, and what happens next

To report a profile, open it, scroll to the bottom, choose Report or Block and Report, and follow the prompts. To report one specific message in a chat, use the three-dot menu on that message. Either way, moderators act faster on specifics: the number they gave you, the platform they named, the wallet they sent.

Already unmatched? The in-app buttons have gone with the match, but the route has not — contact Bumble Support directly with the person's name, your reason for reporting and any screenshots, since the investigation depends on what you can supply. Reports are confidential, so the person will not learn who reported them. You can follow the progress of a report in the Help Hub, though do not expect to be told what moderation action was finally taken.

Take your screenshots before you block, not after.

Money has gone: the first 24 hours

Speed matters more than anything else now, and self-blame is the thing that slows people down most.

  • Telephone your bank immediately. Where a transfer left a UK account through Faster Payments or CHAPS on or after 7 October 2024, reimbursement may be available under the current rules: the maximum is £85,000, firms may apply an excess of up to £100, and a claim must be raised within 13 months. Each claim turns on its own facts, so no outcome is promised.
  • Cryptocurrency, vouchers and gift cards are far harder to unwind, which makes saving wallet addresses, transaction IDs and voucher serial numbers urgent rather than optional.
  • If identity documents or personal details were shared and that exposure puts you at heightened risk of identity fraud, consider Cifas Protective Registration — applications are online at cifas.org.uk/pr. It costs £30 for two years and places a warning flag against your name and other personal details in the National Fraud Database, prompting organisations that use Cifas data to make extra identity checks when those details are used in applications. It does not affect your credit score, but not every application will be checked.
  • File with Report Fraud (reportfraud.police.uk, 0300 123 2040) if you are in England, Wales or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report it to Police Scotland on 101.
  • Tell one person you trust today. Isolation is part of the method, and it also makes every practical step harder to face alone.

Our scam recovery checklist sets out the order to work through. For free, confidential support outside your own circle, contact Victim Support in England and Wales on 0808 168 9111, Victim Support Scotland through victimsupport.scot, or Victim Support NI through victimsupportni.com.

Frequently asked questions

I made the first move, so how could it be a scam?

Scam profiles are built to be swiped right on, not to start conversations. Who sends the first message on Bumble depends on the match and on any Opening Move that has been set; it is not a check on who sits behind the profile. Having opened the chat is neutral evidence, and it may make later warnings feel easier to dismiss.

Can I make a Bumble match prove who they are?

Up to a point. The request you can send in the app asks a match to complete Photo Verification — a selfie check that they match their profile photos. ID Verification, which uses a government-issued document plus a live selfie, is separate and optional in the UK. Neither proves intentions or financial claims, and because both are voluntary an absent badge proves little on its own. A refusal alongside declarations of love is still informative.

My match says reply now or we will expire. Is that a warning sign?

On its own, no — a Bumble match expires if no one sends a message within 24 hours of matching, so the timer is a normal rule. Paired with pressure to move to WhatsApp before the countdown ends, yes. One free Extend a day, plus Rematch on Boost and Premium, means a lapsed match is not a lost one.

Doesn't Deception Detector remove the fake profiles for me?

Not reliably. Bumble says that in testing it automatically blocked 95 per cent of the accounts it had identified as spam or scam profiles — the denominator is accounts Bumble had already identified, not every fraudulent account. No automated tool guarantees that a profile is safe, and screening is weakest against one patient human who does nothing unusual for weeks.

How do I report someone on Bumble after unmatching?

The in-app buttons go with the match, so contact Bumble Support instead, giving the person's name, your reason and any screenshots or payment details you kept. You can check the report's progress in the Help Hub. Where money was lost, report to Report Fraud as well, or to Police Scotland on 101 if you are in Scotland.
